newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S, China chart future course.
newsitem.headline: U.S, China chart future course.

text.p: The United States and China, after years of turmoil, have crafted a blueprint for working cooperatively into the next century -- but no doubt it will be tested often.

Their long, hard climb back from the abyss of constant confrontation, angry rhetoric, cancelled meetings and unpredictable behaviour was confirmed this week during U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's visit to Beijing.

While there were no dramatic breakthroughs announced, the two sides were upbeat after the talks, saying they established a firm basis for moving forward on a wide range of issues, including extremely contentious ones.

This is expected to manifest itself on Sunday when U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin meet here on the fringes of the Asia Pacific Economic forum. A timetable, if not specific dates, for an exchange of summits in each other's capitals is likely to be announced.

Experts have warned for some time that with China fast rising to the U.S. level of economic -- and maybe political and military -- power, Washington had better find a steady way of managing a vital relationship that had been subjected to too many position reversals and was in a dangerous downward spiral.
China, too big and important to ignore, must be taken seriously and integrated into the international economic and political system at every opportunity, they argue.
"Now more than ever before the American and Chinese people can and must work together to advance our interests," Christopher said in a speech on Thursday in Shanghai.

The new approach, which also serves China's need to be a major international player, includes a commitment to hold frequent high-level meetings and keep talking, regardless of how sharply the two sides disagree on such topics as Taiwan.
That was how the United States dealt with the Soviet Union in the Cold War, despite nuclear arms targeted at each other's cities and huge rows over human rights and other issues.

But after China waged a bloody military crackdown in 1989 on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, an engagement largely cultivated since then-President Richard Nixon's opening to China in 1971 was shattered.

Washington imposed sanctions. When Bill Clinton first took office in 1992, the inexperenced president intensified strains by demanding Beijing meet certain human rights standards before receiving trade benefits enjoyed by most other countries.
He dropped that linkage in 1994, then stumbled again badly by granting a visa in 1995 to the president of Taiwan, the nationalist island communist China considers a renegade regime.

The Chinese were angry, increasingly hostile and mistrustful. So were the Americans. Congress, divided over China, played a huge role in whipsawing U.S. policy while the adminstration seemed unsure of its aims and strategy.

About 15 months ago, the two governments reached out to each other. Finally this week, after much hard work on both sides, Christopher returned to Beijing, determined to leave his predecessor a clean slate. His last trip to the Chinese capital in 1994 turned disastrous over human rights differences.
The Americans seemed to try harder. In a major shift, Christopher toned down his public comments on human rights, despite Beijing's recent intensified repression of dissidents.
China's record remains a matter of grave concern but bilateral ties cannot be held hostage to one issue, he said.

U.S. officials have gone out of their way not to overreact to persistent new charges from U.S. intelligence sources in recent months that China has violated this or that commitment not to sell missiles, conventional arms and nuclear technology to states viewed as troublesome like Iran.

Officials say they have no proof of recent violations and stress increased Chinese cooperation on matters of concern, including North Korea and this week's promise to establish a nationwide system of export controls.
In return, Washington opened the door to letting China buy limited kinds of nuclear assistance for peaceful uses from American firms before a 1985 accord is finally put into effect.

Critics worry the administration may now be too eager to make near-term concessions in return for mere promises. U.S. officials insist they are vigilant but their eagerness to advance ties with Beijing is palpable.
They debated calling the new relationship a "partnership" but dropped the idea when cooler heads decided the term greatly exaggerates the current state of play between the two states.
